s4.text: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy complication marked by new high blood pressure and signs of organ damage, usually appearing after the 20th week.
Women having their first baby, those carrying twins, and those with obesity or chronic kidney disease face a higher risk of preeclampsia.
Magnesium sulfate is given intravenously to women with severe preeclampsia to prevent seizures, and it remains the treatment of choice for eclampsia.
Worldwide, preeclampsia affects roughly two to eight percent of pregnancies and is a leading cause of maternal and newborn illness.
The only definitive cure for preeclampsia is delivery of the baby and placenta, although the timing depends on gestational age and severity.
Eclampsia refers to the onset of seizures in a woman with preeclampsia that cannot be attributed to another cause.
Low-dose aspirin started before 16 weeks of pregnancy can lower the chance of preeclampsia in women judged to be at high risk.
The term eclampsia comes from a Greek word meaning a sudden flash, reflecting the abrupt seizures described by ancient physicians.
Researchers believe preeclampsia begins with abnormal development of the blood vessels that supply the placenta early in pregnancy.
Women who have had preeclampsia are more likely to develop heart disease and stroke later in life, so long-term follow-up is advised.
Labetalol, nifedipine and hydralazine are commonly used to bring blood pressure down quickly in women with preeclampsia.
Doctors screen for preeclampsia at every prenatal visit by checking blood pressure and testing the urine for protein.
Preeclampsia can occasionally develop after childbirth, usually within the first week, a condition known as postpartum preeclampsia.
Before magnesium sulfate became standard care in the twentieth century, eclampsia was one of the most feared causes of maternal death.
Blood tests measuring the sFlt-1 to PlGF ratio can help doctors predict which women are likely to develop preeclampsia within a week.
Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar that develops during pregnancy and is usually detected with a glucose tolerance test between 24 and 28 weeks.
Placenta previa occurs when the placenta covers part or all of the cervix, often causing painless bright red bleeding late in pregnancy.
Hyperemesis gravidarum is persistent, intense vomiting in pregnancy that can lead to dehydration, weight loss and hospital admission.
An ectopic pregnancy happens when a fertilized egg implants outside the uterus, most often in one of the fallopian tubes.
Preterm labor is defined as regular contractions that open the cervix before 37 completed weeks of pregnancy.
Rh incompatibility can occur when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby, and an injection of anti-D immunoglobulin helps prevent problems.
Morning sickness affects most pregnant women during the first trimester and usually eases by the fourteenth to sixteenth week.
